summary: Final issue of South Korean Interim Government Activities, covering July-August 1948 and prepared by the National Economic Board's Statistics Division. It records the 15 August 1948 establishment of the Republic of Korea, the end of USAMGIK (succeeded by the Civil Affairs Section, USAFIK) and the continuing SKIG wind-down. The Summary and the retrospective passages review three years of occupation: population movement, vested property, agriculture and fertilizer, industry under the loss of northern electric power (cut 14 May), trade, labor, transport, finance, law, police, health, education, press, youth and women. Political chapters cover the Constitution, Government Organization Law, National Assembly, Rhee's cabinet and party history. Historians will find extensive statistics (refugees, prices, production, trade, deposits, budgets), the vested-property handover, the Torture Case against the police, the floods, and candid official assessments of occupation achievements and limits.
highlights: The Republic of Korea was proclaimed on 15 August 1948, ending USAMGIK, which was succeeded by the Civil Affairs Section, USAFIK; Rhee Syngman was elected President 180 votes of 196 and Lee Bum-suk approved Prime Minister 110-84.

After the Soviet cutoff of northern electric power on 14 May, anthracite output fell from 68,612 tons in April to 38,887 in July, though power deliveries held at about 56 million KWH in July and August.

Population movement since October 1945 saw 2,454,480 arrivals, including 1,115,550 Koreans from Japan and 622,044 from North Korea, against 886,618 departures, mostly Japanese; estimated population was 20.3 million on 1 July 1948.
Vested property had net worth of 85,849,975 thousand won; 35 of 5,358 investigated companies passed to elected boards from 10 July, and 481,957 acres of farmland were sold to farmers by 31 July.
The 1948 crop was estimated near 6,000,000 metric tons, the highest since 1941, helped by over 548,000 tons of fertilizer imports since October 1946, though July floods inundated 504,541 acres.
The SKIG overdraft reached 22,506 million won, note issue stood at 30,000 million won, and the urban retail price index (1947 = 100) rose from 86 in January 1947 to 179 in August 1948.

The Torture Case, a January death at Metropolitan Police Division M leaked in July, led Detective Bureau chiefs Lee Man-chong and Cho Byung-sul to resign on 12 August; Chief Chang Taik-sang survived a fourth attempt on his life on 24 July.
Korean National Youth reached 1,154,821 members and donated over 12,600,000 work days, and Korea competed under its own flag at the London Olympics, finishing 24th with 15 points.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, National Economic Board members under Chairman Wilhelm Anderson, Statistics Division contributors, Arthur G. Peterson's foreword on the Republic's 15 August founding and the series since 1946, and the table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Chairman Anderson reviews three years of occupation: refugee growth, near food self-sufficiency from fertilizer imports, trade deficit cut from 400 to 25 per cent, the 14 May northern power cutoff, vested property, and an overdraft above 22,000 million won.

sections.title: Part I. Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Covers population and refugee movement (886,618 outbound, 2,454,480 inbound since 1945) and vested property worth 85,849,975 thousand won net, with 35 companies transferred to elected boards.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugee, repatriation and population statistics through August 1948, including 151 Turk-Tartars granted Turkish visas, an estimated 20.3 million population on 1 July 1948, and the Population and Census Committee.

sections.title: Refugees
sections.summary: National Refugee Board created 12 May 1947. Table 1 counts 185,441 refugees in 1946, 163,235 in 1947 and 86,036 to mid-August 1948; Seoul entry was barred from 1 July 1947.

sections.title: Repatriation
sections.summary: Since October 1945, 886,618 left (mostly Japanese) and 2,454,480 arrived, including 1,115,550 Koreans from Japan and 622,044 from North Korea; 596,780 Koreans remain in Japan.

sections.title: Emigration of Stateless Turk-Tartars
sections.summary: Turkey issued visas in August 1948 to 151 stateless Turk-Tartars (97 adults, 54 children) from Seoul, Pusan and Inchon; the project passed to the Republic's Foreign Ministry, with sailing expected by end of October.

sections.title: Statistical Analysis of Population in South Korea
sections.summary: George Deihl's analysis of 1947 registrations estimates about 887,000 births (44.35 per thousand), 260,000 deaths and 3.1 per cent natural increase, a 1 July 1948 population of 20.3 million, and life expectancy of 45 to 49.

sections.title: Population and Census Committee
sections.summary: Committee on Population and Census Statistics, set up 4 March 1948, coordinated SKIG data and projected population from 20,100,000 on 31 March 1948 to 21,000,000 by 31 December 1949.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody prepared handover to Koreans: net vested worth 85,849,975 thousand won, July sales of 199 properties, 1,119 claims cases, loan guarantees, and 35 companies transferred to elected boards.

sections.title: Operations
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody reorganized for handover: seven-section Administrative Division, Purchase and Contract Board for deals over 200,000 won, gasoline cut 50 per cent. Vested holdings were 256,019,630 thousand won gross, 85,849,975 thousand net.

sections.title: Property Disposal
sections.summary: July sales of 199 properties brought 217,870 thousand won; 957 sales worth 1,918,888 thousand won since August 1947. Inspections covered Taegu and Pusan textile mills and 355 vessels at Mokpo and Kunsan.

sections.title: Real Estate Transfers
sections.summary: Five USAFIK properties, including CIC Headquarters in Inchon and the Sugar Bowl Building, were regularized. The largest army property release yet included 149 dependent houses, 117 buildings at Camp Taejon and a 19-building Pusan Navy Compound.

sections.title: Policy Decisions and Claims Section
sections.summary: OPC Memorandum No. 32 of 12 August treated Allied-owned companies organized in Japan as Allied, not vested. Claims Section at 31 August: 1,119 cases, 453 allowed, 233 disallowed, 531 pending.

sections.title: Comptroller Activities and Corporate Affairs
sections.summary: Property Custodian guaranteed loans of 7,000,000 won to Chosun Tanning and 5,000,000 won to Korean Fisheries. Statements for 1,812 companies show 1,021,121 thousand won profit; 35 of 5,358 investigated companies went to elected boards, starting 10 July.

sections.title: Part II. Production and Supply
sections.summary: Covers food, prices, industry, mining, distribution, trade and labor: 1948 crop near 6,000,000 tons, retail index 179, anthracite down to 38,887 tons in July, $328 million civilian supply imports, and Pusan wage disputes.

sections.title: Section 1. Food and Agriculture
sections.summary: 1948 crop near 6,000,000 tons, highest since 1941; floods affected 504,541 acres; fertilizer imports exceeded 548,000 tons; 481,957 acres of vested farmland sold to farmers by 31 July.

sections.title: Food
sections.summary: The 1948 crop estimate of almost 6,000,000 metric tons is the highest since 1941, with self-sufficiency expected from January 1949. Summer grain collection reached 95.8 per cent of quota; stocks were 244,169 tons at end of August.

sections.title: Floods
sections.summary: The 7 July typhoon broke 801 Cholla levees, damaged 28,219 acres and killed 75. Table 8 lists 504,541 acres flooded, mostly in Cholla-pukto; crops were replanted and forecasts stayed above 1947.

sections.title: Agricultural Bureaus and Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Rice transplanting finished two weeks early. Raw silk fell to 121.5 tons for lack of coal, power and cocoons; chick hatching reached 605,470 of a 2,000,000 goal; fishing landings were 67 per cent of 1947.

sections.title: Korea Agricultural Association
sections.summary: Korea Agricultural Association shipped 5,200,000 straw grain bags for export to Japan despite floods. Directives of 10 and 28 July set ammonium sulphate at 370 won per bag; 424,970 tons were sold to farmers.

sections.title: Agricultural Improvement Service
sections.summary: Fertilizer imports since October 1946 exceeded 548,000 metric tons by end of August 1948. Extension work trained over 1,000 myun agents and promoted disease-free potatoes and second-crop planting.

sections.title: National Land Administration
sections.summary: Ordinance No. 215 of 10 August amended the Land Administration's ordinance. By 31 July 85 per cent of available farms were sold: 502,224 farms and 481,957 acres; rent collection reached 25 per cent.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Prices resumed rising after five months of stability. A new weighted index of urban workers' retail prices (1947 = 100) rose from 86 in January 1947 to 179 in August 1948.

sections.title: Index Numbers of Retail Prices Paid by Urban Workers
sections.summary: New weighted index (1947 = 100) replaced the unweighted Bank of Chosun series, weighting foods 57.5, utilities 21.9 and clothing 15.1. It rose from 86 in January 1947 to 179 in August 1948, using 32 series from nine cities.

sections.title: Section 3. Industrial Production
sections.summary: Output fell under restricted power: flour 1,782 tons in August, cotton yarn up 22 per cent in July, nails up 46 per cent, no cement in July, insulators down to 4,800 pieces, salt 4,808 tons.

sections.title: Processed Food and Textiles
sections.summary: One of two large vested flour mills had power; flour output was 707 tons in July and 1,782 in August versus 1,653 in June. Cotton yarn rose 22 per cent in July and cloth 34 per cent.

sections.title: Paper, Hardware and Chemicals
sections.summary: Power shortage depressed paper, chemicals and building materials. The best paper mill idled for lack of sulphite pulp, nail output rose 46 per cent in July, and no cement was made in July.

sections.title: Miscellaneous and Monopoly Bureau
sections.summary: Electric insulators fell to 4,800 pieces in July and 1,500 in early August; pencils rose 22 per cent to 4,400 gross. Monopoly Bureau salt fell to 4,808 tons and cigarettes to 108.3 tons.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: After the Soviet power cut of 14 May, anthracite fell from 68,612 tons in April to 38,887 in July. August allocations: 28,844 tons to Commerce, 26,000 to Army. Coal imports from Japan hit 104,055 tons in July.

sections.title: Section 5. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: National Consumer Goods Office processed 1,095 allocations worth 2,184,468,531 won by 31 August; petroleum, salt and North Korean barter reported, including 950,861,250 won of northern imports to 15 August.

sections.title: National Consumer Goods Office
sections.summary: Created by Executive Order No. 12 of 12 January 1948 under Dr. Chyung Yil-heung, it had processed 1,095 allocations worth 2,184,468,531 won by 31 August, 88.7 per cent for special groups and 28.2 per cent to farmers.

sections.title: Distribution of Controlled Commodities
sections.summary: The Federation of Financial Associations, over 600 branches and nearly 2,000,000 members, distributes goods on a 15 per cent commission. Eligible employees numbered 480,273, up 43,630 since June.

sections.title: Petroleum
sections.summary: Gasoline deliveries were 4,901,333 liters in July and 6,079,399 in August against allocations above 7,000,000, short mainly because the Pusan terminal could not fill drums.

sections.title: Salt Distribution
sections.summary: Government salterns made 65,323 tons in F/Y 1947. For F/Y 1948, 68,774 tons (58.6 per cent of the 134,631-ton goal) were made by 15 August; stocks of 184,170 tons allowed full rations.

sections.title: Barter Trade with North Korea
sections.summary: Commerce Order No. 4 (2 August 1948) legalized overland barter with North Korea. Northern imports totalled 950,861,250 won January to 15 August, notably dried fish; contracts worth 382,499,000 won were pending.

sections.title: Section 6. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private trade in seven months of 1948 was 3,600 million won imports and 2,700 million exports; government trade with Japan totalled $8,377,383 since 1945, and civilian supply imports reached $328,117,607.

sections.title: Private Trade Statistics
sections.summary: June imports were 436,652,000 won and exports 286,673,000; July imports 431,060,000 and exports 345,916,000. Inchon handled over 59 per cent of January-July trade; Hong Kong took most exports.

sections.title: Private Trade Activities
sections.summary: Six commercial shipping companies (three American, two British, one Dutch) ran regularly by August 1948; Hong Kong-Pusan freight was HK$65 per ton. Fifteen businessmen were cleared to investigate trade.

sections.title: Government-to-Government Transactions
sections.summary: Exports to Japan totalled $8,377,383 since 1945, $828,457 of it in July-15 August, chiefly 3,329,070 straw bags and graphite. Pusan exported 15,141 tons; China allowed no exports.

sections.title: Korean Items for Americans in Korea
sections.summary: Army Exchange Service bought 160,789 Korean units worth $223,063 through 15 August 1948, mainly jewelry, brassware, lacquerware and silk. July sales were $4,857, the lowest since August 1947.

sections.title: Civilian Supply Imports
sections.summary: Imports since September 1945 totalled $328,117,607, including GARIOA foodstuffs of $110,446,030 by June. Coal from Japan reached a record 104,055 tons in July; July salt imports were 19,609 tons.

sections.title: Section 7. Labor
sections.summary: Covers wage policy (Wage Stabilization Division, 25 March 1948), Pusan stevedore dispute over a 500-won daily wage, Yongwol Mines election won by Tai Han with 2,099 votes, and bank overtime violations.

sections.title: Wage Problems
sections.summary: Traces wage policy from the 25 June 1946 hold-the-line stance to the Wage Stabilization Division of 25 March 1948. A 3 July 1948 directive restricted general raises; a critical appraisal found no enforcement.

sections.title: General Current Activities and Labor Relations
sections.summary: Pusan stevedores threatened a strike over a 500-won daily wage demand; talks on 22 July set a 350-won minimum, but a coal pier stoppage followed on 7 August. Marine Bureau contract for about 1,500 workers was agreed except wages.

sections.title: Unions, Standards, Health and Education
sections.summary: Tai Han won the Yongwol Mines election of 8 July with 2,099 votes; its executive committee resigned after the Chun Jin-han motion failed 44 to 22. Bank overtime violations left 15,654 won owing to 158 employees.

sections.title: Part III. Public Services
sections.summary: Covers rail (2,145 operating miles, 268 operable engines), marine, highway and air transport; 37,183 telephones; power deliveries of 56.2 million KWH in July; and public works, including 517 bridges rebuilt.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: Department of Transportation covers railroads (August receipts 578 million won against 737 million expenditures), the Marine Bureau's 12 LSTs and 11 Freight Supply vessels, and highway and air transport.

sections.title: Railroads
sections.summary: The rail system taken over in September 1945 had 2,145 operating miles. Operable engines fell from 300 to 268 by August 1948; August receipts were 578 million won against 737 million expenditures, with 31,894 employed.

sections.title: Marine Transportation
sections.summary: Marine Bureau history: merged into the Bureau of Transportation in 1942; sham ship sales to Koreans were voided after liberation; 12 LSTs and 11 Freight Supply vessels were bought; Rainbow service began in 1948.

sections.title: Highway and Air Transportation
sections.summary: Highway transport ran from the 1944 Pan-Korean Trucking Union (80 per cent Japanese-owned) to the Korean Truck Co. of December 1945, disbanded July 1946. Highway employment had fallen to 46 and air to 27.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: July revenue of 88.9 million won was a post-liberation high. Reports 37,183 telephones with 10,000 applications unserved, 623 post offices, and 11 radio stations with a 100-won monthly fee from 1 August.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: Power deliveries were 56.2 million KWH in July and 55.7 million in August after the 14 May northern cutoff. Yong Wol was separated from the Korea Electric Power Company on 26 July; the Giroux mission report of 23 July is quoted.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: Public works rebuilt 517 bridges, 1,422 km of road and 162 km of levees. Floods caused over 2,000 million won damage; 800 million won was sought for repairs, and an Emergency Water Conservation Board was set up 26 July.

sections.title: Part IV. Finance
sections.summary: Government finance shows note issue of 30,000 million won, overdraft of 22,506 million and appropriations of 35,264 million; non-government finance shows deposits of 43,335 million and loans of 30,038 million through July.

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: Note issue was 30,000 million won at end-August against a 33,400 million peak; the overdraft was 22,506 million. August revenue was 2,157 million against 1,924 million expenditure; appropriations totaled 35,264 million.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Through July 1948, deposits reached 43,335 million won, 57 per cent from the public, with loans of 30,038 million (70 per cent of deposits). Life insurance in force was 1,067 million won; damage insurers wrote 9,243 policies.

sections.title: Part V. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Records the Republic's proclamation on 15 August 1948, Rhee's inauguration on 24 July, the Constitution of 12 July, Lee Bum-suk's approval as Prime Minister 110-84, legal ordinances, the Torture Case, and party history.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: Proclamation of the Republic (Tai Han Min Kook) on 15 August 1948 ended Military Government. Covers the 10 May election and Rhee's 24 July inauguration; Military Government personnel fell to 2,870 by 15 August.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Developments
sections.summary: Constitution and Government Organization Law, Rhee elected President 180 to 196, Lee Bum-suk approved Prime Minister 110-84, cabinet completed by 6 August, moderates' split, and party development since liberation.

sections.title: Constitution and Government Organization Law
sections.summary: The Constitution passed unanimously on 12 July, with a strong presidency, four-year Assembly and farmland to tillers. The Government Organization Law of 16 July created eleven departments, an Economic Board and Civil Service and Inspection Committees.

sections.title: National Assembly
sections.summary: Rhee was elected President 180 votes of 196 on 20 July; Lee Bum-suk was approved Prime Minister 110-84 after Lee Yun-yung was rejected 132-59. Kim Byung-no was confirmed Chief Justice 117-31.

sections.title: Republic of Korea
sections.summary: Rhee's cabinet was completed by 6 August. The Republic was proclaimed on 15 August; General Hodge said Americans would only advise, and transfers began 16 August. The press called the cabinet mediocre and partisan.

sections.title: Moderate Activities
sections.summary: Chough Pyung-ok became ambassador-at-large and Chang Myun chief UN delegate in Paris. Moderates split three ways; Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic held to unified independence, Kimm wavering after meeting Lee Bum-suk on 10 August.

sections.title: Summary (political parties)
sections.summary: Three blocs emerged: communists, extreme rightists and moderates under Kimm Kiu-sic. Ordinance No. 55 of February 1946 produced over 400 Seoul parties; Rhee gained power as Kim Koo defected.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Ordinances Nos. 203-219 drafted 1 July-31 August, four Department of Justice opinions, court caseloads (90,112 cases in 1947), Cheju-do riot trials, and prison population of 22,321 in July.

sections.title: Ordinances and Orders
sections.summary: Ordinances Nos. 203-219 drafted 1 July-31 August covered litigation fees, taxicabs, the bar, rice collection, National Land Administration suits and school districts. 26 American lawyers were admitted to the Korean bar.

sections.title: Legal Opinions
sections.summary: Four Department of Justice opinions: Japanese repatriates' pension deposits (No. 1627), the Chosun Mining Development Corporation (No. 1612), narcotics informer awards (No. 1650), and the metric system as official but not exclusive (No. 1633).

sections.title: Korean Courts
sections.summary: Cheju-do riot trials were stalled, with about 250 held; the Military Governor allowed transfer to Mokpo or Kwangju. Courts heard 67,181 cases in 1946 and 90,112 in 1947; a Kunsan branch opened.

sections.title: Penal Institutions
sections.summary: Prison population was 22,141 in April and 22,321 in July, about 45 per cent for theft or burglary. The juvenile house of correction held 541 in June and 664 in July; 174 guards graduated in June.

sections.title: Section 4. National Police
sections.summary: Covers the Torture Case, the 24 July attack on Chief Chang Taik-sang, Detective Bureau resignations of 12 August, Seoul crime statistics, and the police's retrospective, including over 120 policemen killed by October 1946.

sections.title: Torture Case
sections.summary: Suspect Lim Wha was tortured to death at Metropolitan Police Division M in January. The Detective Bureau leaked it in July; Chief Detective Ro Duk-sul reportedly confessed and escaped on 27 July. No prosecutor decision by August.

sections.title: Attack on Chief Chang
sections.summary: Three men fired on Chang Taik-sang's car in Yongdungpo on 24 July, the fourth attempt on his life; Chang was unhurt. Detective Bureau chiefs Lee Man-chong and Cho Byung-sul resigned 12 August.

sections.title: Summary (National Police)
sections.summary: Police separated from National Defense in April 1946 and endured riots from January 1946 to Taegu in October 1946, with over 120 policemen killed. Economic and Sanitation Bureaus were eliminated; a special Inspection Command serves Cheju-do.

sections.title: Section 5. Inter-Zone Activities
sections.summary: Mail crossed the 38th parallel on 9 trips in July-August 1948. Commerce Order No. 4 of 2 August required permits and bonds for barter. An American soldier was killed on 19 July; Radio Pyongyang promoted the 25 August election.

sections.title: Part VI. Social
sections.summary: Covers flood relief (254,664 persons needy), 14,989,286 textbooks, three education ordinances of 12 August, 58 dailies, Korean National Youth's 1,154,821 members, women's equality, and the 1948 London Olympics.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Cholera deaths fell from over 15,000 in 1946 to 10 in 1947 through immunization. Flood relief reached 254,664 needy persons; UNRRA granted 2,700,000 won in July and 6,135,000 won in August.

sections.title: Public Assistance
sections.summary: Flood damage: 3,604 houses washed away, 14,881 crushed, 254,664 persons made needy. 1,149 tents went to refugees; UNRRA granted 2,700,000 won in July and 6,135,000 won in August.

sections.title: Summary (Public Health and Welfare)
sections.summary: Cholera deaths fell from over 15,000 in 1946 to 10 in 1947 through mass immunization. The Department also opened the first venereal disease clinic and moved the Chung Nyang Ni asylum to medical supervision on 1 July.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Three ordinances effective 12 August created school districts, nine-member boards and local school taxation. 7,500 teachers trained, including 500 at Kwanju; 14,989,286 textbooks published since liberation; Teacher Training Center of 400 with 20 American educators.

sections.title: Section 3. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: In July Korea had 58 dailies, 67 weeklies and 125 monthlies. The press covered the new government, the North Korean election of 25 August, floods, Cheju-do riots and the Dok Do bombing.

sections.title: Formation of New Government
sections.summary: Papers backed Assembly rejection of Lee Yun-yung and approval of Lee Bum-suk, and feared a separate Police Department, defeated 108 to 88. Seoul Shin Mun led circulation at 76,000 among 58 dailies.

sections.title: Floods, Cheju-do Riots and Dok Do Incident
sections.summary: The press protested the North Korean election of 25 August. Floods and typhoon cost an estimated 2,000,000,000 won, with 169 killed in Cholla-namdo; papers demanded more than 2,480,000 won reparations for the Dok Do bombing.

sections.title: Foreign News and Editorials
sections.summary: Foreign news covered the Berlin crisis and the Cominform's Yugoslav condemnation. Editorials blamed SKIG's failure on military officials and Korean corruption, praised Lee Bum-suk, and criticized the Constitution as too socialistic.

sections.title: Miscellany
sections.summary: The torture row ended when Maj.-Gen. Dean limited police press statements to the police director. Papers exposed Seoul school entrance fees and exaggerated sentences for Koreans in the Kobe and Osaka riots.

sections.title: Section 4. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Chartered 9 October 1945, it reached 1,154,821 audited members by 15 August 1948. Members donated over 12,600,000 work days, planted 6,770,397 trees and trained over 100,000 leaders; Lee Jun-sic succeeded Lee Bum-suk as president.

sections.title: Section 5. Women's Activities
sections.summary: Women gained constitutional equality; the policewoman force numbers 500 and Louise Yim became Minister of Commerce and Industry. Ordinances Nos. 70 and 112 and Executive Order No. 16 outlaw prostitution; the Women's Bureau dates from Ordinance No. 107 of 1946.

sections.title: Section 6. Culture
sections.summary: Hangul returned to schools from October 1945, though Chinese characters persist. The American Language Institute has about 500 students. Korea's 67-man team finished 24th with 15 points at the London Olympics under its own flag.
